Answer
AN-s'r
n. and v. (rendering Hebrew 'ānâh, Greek apokrinomai and apologia)
From Old English andswaru, a swearing against — originally a sworn reply to a charge, which is why the word keeps a legal flavour in English. The Hebrew 'ānâh means to answer, respond, or testify, and its legal sense stands behind the ninth commandment's false witness. The Greek apologia is likewise a courtroom word — a defence spoken in reply to an accusation — and it is the word Peter uses of the Christian's duty to explain his hope.

Biblical Definition

Answer in Scripture is chiefly a question of manner, and the Bible's counsel on it is remarkably practical. Proverbs makes the tone of a reply a moral matter with visible consequences: “A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger” (Pro 15:1). The observation is not that softness is always effective, but that the reply itself is one of the two forces at work in every quarrel, and a man governs one of them. Paul makes the same point a rule of Christian speech and grounds it in preparation rather than instinct: “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man” (Col 4:6) — grace and salt together, so that speech is neither insipid nor corrosive, and the every man forbids the common practice of reserving courtesy for those who deserve it. Peter turns the word to its formal sense and lays a standing obligation on every believer: “But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear” (1Pe 3:15). The requirements are exact — a settled reverence within, a reasoned account, constant readiness, and meekness in the delivery. There is also a time for no answer at all, and the Lord Jesus set the pattern before Pilate and the chief priests: “And when he was accused of the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing” (Mat 27:12). Silence before a court that has already decided is not weakness; it is a form of testimony.

Webster 1828 Definition

A reply to a question, charge, or objection; a defence or account given in reply; and in Scripture the soft answer that turns away wrath, the gracious answer seasoned with salt, and the reasoned answer every believer must be ready to give for his hope.

expand to see more

ANSWER, v. 1. To speak in return to a call or question, or to a speech, declaration or argument.

2. To be accountable, liable or responsible; as, to answer for another's debt.

3. To be equivalent to; to correspond with; as, one thing answers to another.

4. n. A reply; that which is said in return to a question or objection. A soft answer turneth away wrath. Prov. 15.

5. A defence; an account or vindication given in reply, as before a tribunal. Be ready always to give an answer. 1 Pet. 3.

Key Scripture

Proverbs 15:1 — "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger."

Colossians 4:6 — "Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man."

1 Peter 3:15 — "But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:"

Matthew 27:12 — "And when he was accused of the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing."

Modern Corruption

The command to give an answer is treated as optional for ordinary believers and left to specialists, while the manner Scripture attaches to it — meekness and fear — is discarded wherever the argument is thought to be winning.

expand to see more

1Pe 3:15 is addressed to a whole persecuted church, not to a class of trained defenders, and the duty it lays down is universal: be ready always, to every man that asketh. Where this is treated as the province of specialists, two things follow. Ordinary Christians conclude that they need not be able to say why they believe, and their faith becomes inarticulate to themselves as well as to others; and the church's witness contracts to the few occasions when an expert is present. Peter assumes the opposite: that believers living visibly different lives under pressure will be asked, and that the question deserves a reason. The command begins inwardly — sanctify the Lord God in your hearts — because a man who has settled who is Lord within has something to say when the question comes.

The second corruption concerns manner, and it is now the more common failure. The same verse that requires an answer prescribes its temper: with meekness and fear. Contemporary argument, including Christian argument, is conducted largely for the benefit of onlookers who already agree, and rewards the reply that humiliates. Scripture's standard makes that a disqualification rather than a victory, since the servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient, in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves. The principle to recover joins the two halves: an answer that is reasoned but contemptuous has failed the command as surely as no answer at all, and a soft answer is not a weak one — it is the reply that turns away wrath (Pro 15:1) rather than feeding it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'ānâh is to answer, respond, or testify, with a legal sense of replying to a charge. Greek apokrinomai is to reply, and apologia is a formal defence spoken before a tribunal, whence the English apologetics.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'ānâh (H6030) — to answer, respond, testify; used of replying to a question and of bearing witness in a cause.

Hebrew ma'aneh (H4617) — an answer or reply; a soft answer turneth away wrath (Pro 15:1), literally an answer of gentleness.

Greek apokrinomai (G611) — to answer or reply; the ordinary narrative verb, as Jesus answered and said unto them.

Greek apologia (G627) — a verbal defence, a reasoned reply to an accusation; the word in 1Pe 3:15 and in Paul's defence before Agrippa.

Greek eperotēma (G1906) — an enquiry or appeal; the answer of a good conscience toward God (1Pe 3:21), a different sense of the English word.

Usage

"Of the manner of reply: a soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger (Pro 15:1)."

"Of prepared and gracious speech: let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt (Col 4:6)."

"Of the standing duty to explain the hope: be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you (1Pe 3:15)."
